All of these are the issues that multilateralism must address today decisively and without delay. No country or region acting in isolation even with vast medical, technological, or economic resources, will be able to successfully meet the urgent needs of their people in the face of problems that even threaten the very existence of human life. Mr. President, the work of the United Nations to promote health is part of its humanitarian and development work, and that is rooted in its principles and concrete action throughout the world and has been since its founding 80 years ago. There's also the persistent message we've heard time and time again from world leaders who have been able to speak before this General Assembly. That message and the work of the United Nations have been clear and unequivocal. Health cannot be just a privilege for the richest. Neither can it remain a business. Health is a universal right for rich and poor alike, and both states and the United Nations are obliged to ensure that everyone can achieve and enjoy health. In that connection, we take this opportunity to once again condemn the continued enactment, application, and even the ratcheting up of unilateral coercive measures that was seen even during the worst pandemic humanity faced in the past 100 years. And they have been stepped up in spite of the multiple and growing calls for their complete and unconditional elimination. These illegal measures continue to be applied to more than a third of humankind. They constitute real mass violations of the human rights of entire populations. Moreover, they endanger the lives of millions of people. At the same time, they violate on a daily basis the most basic human rights of these people, including the right to health and the right to life. The adoption of the Oslo Declaration reiterates that foreign policy actions in security, trade, conflict, the environment, and human rights have strong bearing on the achievement of national and global health agenda. The spread of COVID-19 has indeed reminded us that the threat to health anywhere is, of course, a threat to health everywhere. For that reason, concerted and coordinated action to advance global health issues in the foreign policy sphere remains essential to our common health equity. The group strongly believes that global health challenges need to be tackled collectively through a robust multilateral health architecture with the WHO as its core and through enhanced partnership, international cooperation, and solidarity. We remain deeply concerned with the ongoing global health inequities and inequalities and emerging challenges such as a lack— such a lack of access to life-saving therapies and antimicrobial resistance, non-communicable diseases, Adverse impact of climate change, extreme weather events, conflicts, and of course humanitarian emergencies. Equity without comprehensively addressing determinants of health. Eliminate structural inequalities, integrate environmental protection into public health priorities, and catalyze regulatory physical measures to support health objectives. Moreover, access to technologies is critical for countries to scale up regional and local production of medicines and health products, which in turn will improve their timely and equitable access and overall the health security for people globally. Third, we share great concerns on the increasing humanitarian emergencies worldwide, which have devastating impact on health systems. Attacks on healthcare contributes to an increased risk of disease outbreaks, worsens malnutrition, and causes excess deaths. The projected workforce shortages by 2030 is increasing due to chronic underinvestment in health workers. The need for increased international focus and investment in the healthcare— in the health workforce, as provided by the WHO Academy, cannot be overlooked in this regard. The group reaffirms our strong commitment to strengthening global health governance, notably To the full and effective implementation of the International Health Regulations, we welcome the adoption of the Pandemic Agreement as a vital legal framework to prepare for future pandemics. Despite these rising challenges, health financing is on the decline, facing sharp cuts on external aid and global health funding. The Foreign Policy and Global Health Initiative remains fully committed to work closely with the WHO, relevant UN entities, and partners to put health front and center of global agenda and strengthen our concerted action in achieving global health equity for all. I thank you, Mr. President.

Noncommunicable diseases and antimicrobial resistance remain at the top of the diplomatic agenda. As the effects of climate change are becoming increasingly apparent, particularly affecting the health of the most vulnerable, and plastic pollution still awaits bold and decisive action from the international community, the One Health approach remains more relevant than ever. The EU and its member states remain firmly committed to promoting health equity and universal health coverage as key enablers, enablers of the 2030 Agenda. The report rightly affirms what many of us know to be true, that global health, foreign policy, and sustainable development are inextricably linked. For Zambia, and indeed for many developing countries, this connection is not abstract. It is a daily reality that defines the well-being and resilience of our people. The COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the structural inequalities in access to vaccines, medicine, and life-saving technologies. Zambia joins others in calling for a truly inclusive and equitable multilateral system, one that prioritizes global solidarity, timely technology transfer, and fairer intellectual property frameworks. No country should be left behind in future health emergencies. We remain deeply concerned by the global stagnation in achieving universal health coverage, Sustainable Development Goal 3.8. Zambia acknowledges that achieving universal health coverage, a specific identified in SDG 3.8 is closely linked to the strength and resilience of its health systems. A well-functioning health system is essential to ensure equitable access to equal quality healthcare services for all, especially in the context of demographic changes, health emergencies, and the increasing burden of non-communicable diseases. Mr. President, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, it's an honor to address this pivotal high-level meeting where global health is rightly framed as a matter of foreign policy and security. emphasized by Agenda Item 127 and Resolution 78/280. This statement aligns with the statement delivered by G77 and China. Mr. President, Timor-Leste sees health as a human right and a vital foundation for peace, stability, and sustainable development. Since independence, we have expanded health— universal health coverage through fortified primary healthcare free essential medicines, and deployment of community health workers across our rural and remote areas, yielding measurable improvements in maternal and child health and vaccination rates. However, today we face a dual health challenge. Communicable diseases may no longer dominate, but the rapid rise of non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular illness, cancers, and chronic respiratory conditions threatens to reverse our progress. Compounding this is the growing burden of mental health conditions worsened by enduring social problems. Such social problems compromise our health system, social cohesion, and development trajectory. Mr. President, we are responding and we are making progress on malaria elimination. As of 24th of July, 2025, Timor-Leste has been certified malaria-free by WHO, becoming the 3rd country in Southeast Asia— or in Asia to win such certification. We salute our health workers and partners who share this journey. On NCD management, we have launched the Timor-Leste HEARTS Programme, aiming to put 50,000 people with hypertension and diabetes on standard care by 2025. Nearly 4% of adults have elevated fasting blood glucose, a key diabetes risk marker, and alarmingly, women face a death rate from diabetes that is 4 times higher than that of men. Moreover, 45% of all deaths in our country are attributed to NCDs. Third, on data and surveillance, we are conducting our second national steps of survey to capture NCD risk factors, including tobacco, alcohol, diet, physical inactivity, raised blood pressure and glucose, and overweight, as well as facility readiness. Innovative digital tools are used for efficient data collection and integrated NCD and mental health services assessments. In mental health integration, despite only a few mental health professionals per 100,000 and a municipal budget allocation, we are embedding psychiatric care into primary health settings for developing a national mental health strategy for 2025-2030. At the local national hospitals in 2020, among those presenting for psychiatric care, schizophrenia accounted for 21%, depression 80%, and suicidal tendencies, 80%— a stark early snapshot of the mental health landscape. Mr. President, however, we acknowledge that we cannot do this alone. As foreign development assistance diminishes, LDCs like Timor-Leste must help mobilize domestic resources. Unaddressed, they will erode stability, widen inequalities, and impair resilience to crises like pandemics and climate change. Bold action, however, can deliver healthier, inclusive, and prosperous societies. Therefore, Timor-Leste calls for: first, stronger international solidarity and predictable financing aligned with universal health coverage. To support the fragile states under unilateral coercive measures, including lifting blockages affecting vulnerable countries like Cuba, Venezuela, and others, and partnership to safeguard our malaria-free status, accelerate NCD and mental health response, and reinforce integrated community health systems. Mr. President, to conclude, Timor-Leste stands ready to partner with the Member States, the WHO, and our development partners to ensure that our collective fight against global health challenges becomes a shared success for humanity. I thank you.
